cards.q: What does javac produce, and what runs it?
cards.a: Bytecode in .class files, which the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) runs.
cards.lessonTitle: Java and the JDK: Your First Program

cards.q: What must the file containing public class Greeter be called?
cards.a: Greeter.java.
cards.lessonTitle: Java and the JDK: Your First Program

cards.q: Why does long population = 8100000000; not compile?
cards.a: The literal is an int literal and is too big for int; write 8_100_000_000L.

cards.q: What is (int) 7.9?
cards.a: 7: casting to int cuts off the fraction.

cards.q: What are 23 / 4 and 23 % 4 for ints?
cards.a: 5 and 3.

cards.q: What does "Sum: " + 1 + 2 print, and how do you get Sum: 3?
cards.a: Sum: 12, because + joins strings left to right; write "Sum: " + (1 + 2).

cards.q: Why does a == b print false for two strings that both contain "hello"?
cards.a: == compares references, and they are different objects; equals compares the text.

cards.q: What is "programming".substring(3, 7)?
cards.a: "gram": from index 3 up to, not including, index 7.

cards.q: What happens in a classic switch case without break?
cards.a: Execution falls through into the next case's statements.

cards.q: What does break outer; do?
cards.a: Leaves the loop labelled outer, including any loops nested inside it.

cards.q: After calling a method that sets its int parameter to 5, has the caller's variable changed?
cards.a: No: Java passes a copy of the value.

cards.q: Can a method change the contents of an array passed to it?
cards.a: Yes: it receives a copy of the reference, which points to the same array.

cards.q: What are the valid indexes of an array of length 5?
cards.a: 0 to 4.

cards.q: Why does System.out.println(array) not show the values?
cards.a: Arrays do not have a readable toString; use Arrays.toString(array).

cards.q: Why can you not write List<int>?
cards.a: Generic collections hold objects only; use the wrapper type List<Integer>.

cards.q: On a List<Integer>, what does list.remove(1) remove?
cards.a: The item at index 1; to remove the value 1, call list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1)).

cards.q: What two parts does every recursive method need?
cards.a: A base case answered directly, and a recursive case that moves toward the base case.

cards.q: Why is the plain recursive Fibonacci slow?
cards.a: It recomputes the same values many times; the number of calls grows exponentially.

cards.q: Why build a long string in a loop with StringBuilder rather than +=?
cards.a: Strings are immutable, so += copies the whole string every time; StringBuilder appends in place.

cards.q: What is '7' - '0' and why?
cards.a: 7: characters are numbers, and the digits '0' to '9' are consecutive codes.

cards.q: What is the difference between a class and an object?
cards.a: A class is the blueprint; an object is one instance made from it with new, with its own field values.

cards.q: What does this.name = name; do in a constructor?
cards.a: Copies the parameter name into the object's field called name.

cards.q: Why make fields private instead of public?
cards.a: So only the class's own methods can change them, keeping the object valid; callers cannot set nonsense values.

cards.q: Can a static method use this?
cards.a: No: a static method belongs to the class and runs without any object.

cards.q: Which version of an overridden method runs: the variable's type or the object's class?
cards.a: The object's class, decided at run time.

cards.q: Why must equals and hashCode be overridden together?
cards.a: Hash-based collections find objects by hash code first; equal objects with different hash codes would be treated as different.

cards.q: Can you create an object of an abstract class?
cards.a: No; only of concrete subclasses that implement every abstract method.

cards.q: Why must a method implementing an interface method be public?
cards.a: Interface methods are implicitly public, and an implementation may not reduce visibility.

cards.q: What does a record generate for record Point(int x, int y)?
cards.a: Private final fields, a constructor, accessors x() and y(), and equals, hashCode and toString based on the values.

cards.q: Why can a switch over a sealed interface leave out default?
cards.a: The compiler knows every permitted subtype, so it can check that all are handled.

cards.q: Why can't you pass a List<Integer> where a List<Number> is expected?
cards.a: The method could add a Double to it through the List<Number> type, breaking the list of integers.

cards.q: Which parameter type lets a method add Integers to a list of Integers, Numbers or Objects?
cards.a: List<? super Integer>.

cards.q: Which set keeps the items sorted?
cards.a: TreeSet.

cards.q: What does map.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum) do?
cards.a: Puts 1 if the word is not yet a key, otherwise adds 1 to its current value.

cards.q: When do you use a Comparator instead of Comparable?
cards.a: When you need an order other than the class's natural order, or the class has none (or you cannot change it).

cards.q: Why is return a.score - b.score; a risky compareTo?
cards.a: The subtraction can overflow for large values and give the wrong sign; Integer.compare cannot.

cards.q: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions?
cards.a: Checked exceptions must be caught or declared with throws; unchecked ones (RuntimeException subclasses) need not be.

cards.q: What does try-with-resources guarantee?
cards.a: Every resource declared in it is closed when the block ends, whether normally or by an exception, in reverse order.

cards.q: Why read a large file with Files.lines or a BufferedReader instead of readAllLines?
cards.a: They read one line at a time instead of loading the whole file into memory.

cards.q: Why must a BufferedWriter be closed?
cards.a: Writing is buffered; closing flushes the remaining data to the file (and releases it).

cards.q: What is the Big O of 5n² + 100n + 7?
cards.a: O(n²): the fastest-growing term dominates, and constants are ignored.

cards.q: Why is a loop that calls list.contains on an ArrayList inside it often O(n²)?
cards.a: contains scans the list, O(n), and it runs once per iteration of an O(n) loop.

cards.q: Why is binary search O(log n)?
cards.a: Each comparison halves the range that can contain the target.

cards.q: What does it mean that merge sort is stable, and which line makes it so?
cards.a: Equal items keep their original order; taking from the left half when a[i] <= a[j] does that.

cards.q: Why is get(i) O(n) for a linked list?
cards.a: There is no index: you must follow i links from the head.

cards.q: Which cases must remove handle besides a node in the middle?
cards.a: Removing the head, removing the tail (updating tail), a one-node list, and a value that is not there.

cards.q: Why does doubling the capacity make ArrayList.add amortised O(1)?
cards.a: Copies happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, ..., n, which add up to less than 2n copies for n adds.

cards.q: What happens to a hash table's speed if every key has the same hashCode?
cards.a: All entries share one bucket, so lookups scan a list: O(n).

cards.q: What does an in-order traversal of a BST produce?
cards.a: The keys in sorted order.

cards.q: Why can inserting 1, 2, 3, ..., n into a plain BST be slow?
cards.a: Each new key becomes the right child of the last, so the tree is a long chain of height n and operations become O(n).

cards.q: What makes an interface usable with a lambda?
cards.a: It has exactly one abstract method: it is a functional interface.

cards.q: Which functional interface fits "takes a String, returns true or false"?
cards.a: Predicate<String>.

cards.q: What happens if a stream pipeline has no terminal operation?
cards.a: Nothing runs: intermediate operations are lazy.

cards.q: What does Collectors.groupingBy(Person::city, Collectors.counting()) produce?
cards.a: A Map from each city to the number of people in it.

cards.q: What is the difference between orElse and orElseGet?
cards.a: orElse always evaluates its default; orElseGet only calls its supplier when the Optional is empty.

cards.q: Where should Optional be used?
cards.a: As the return type of methods that may have no result; not for fields or parameters.

cards.q: Why can two threads incrementing the same int lose updates?
cards.a: count++ is a read, an add and a write; the threads' steps can interleave so both write the same new value.

cards.q: What does future.get() do?
cards.a: Waits until the task has finished and returns its result (or throws if the task failed).

cards.q: In which folder does the class com.example.planner.model.Event live?
cards.a: src/main/java/com/example/planner/model/Event.java (in a Maven or Gradle project).

cards.q: Which members of a class can a class in another package use?
cards.a: Only public ones (and protected ones from subclasses); package-private members are hidden.
